title: The pre-speech placebo is significant and larger than the speech-day effect, so the speech-day coefficient cannot be read as the effect of the speech.
summary: The robustness section says the backing ratio did not predict the VIX change in the two days before the speech, but the printed placebo is significant and larger than the speech-day estimate. A speech cannot move the VIX before it is given, so something correlated with the backing ratio, such as contestation of the framework already under way, can produce both the backing and the speech-day rise.
excerpt: Third, consistent with the expectation that the speech is not made public until the date and time denoted on the transcript, the BR did not predict market uncertainty for the two-day event window before the day of the speech (β = .041, σ2 = 0.017, p = .017, adjusted R-squared = 0.083).
why: For a theory-testing paper, the placebo is the one test that separates an effect of the speech from reverse causality, and as printed it favors reverse causality.
settle: Estimate and plot the backing-ratio coefficient for each day from t-5 to t+5 with the Model 2 controls, test whether t0 exceeds the pre-speech days, re-estimate Model 2 with the pre-speech VIX path from t-5 to t-1 as a control, and correct the p. 25 sentence.

title: No analysis separates the proposed mechanism (lost taken-for-grantedness) from the reading that backing paragraphs carry policy news.
summary: The coding rule counts discussion of the boundaries of policy objectives and tools as backing, during years when those tools and goals changed, and one illustrative backing paragraph discusses a pending change. Unpriced news raises implied volatility, so a news-arrival model predicts the main result equally well, and no reported analysis tells the two apart.
excerpt: In this context, reaffirming the assumptions that underlie the monetary policy framework likely does not provide new information, but rather, presumably seeks to clarify and increase the “signal to noise ratio” in the Fed’s communications (Walsh, 2001; Blinder, 2009; Plosser, 2012), thereby intendedly reducing uncertainty in the market.
why: A theory-testing paper has to show that its evidence favors its mechanism over a standard alternative, and the main estimate alone does not.
settle: Split the backing ratio into restatement and change-discussing paragraph shares and report both coefficients, estimate Model 2 separately for 1998-2007 and 2008-2014, and report VIX changes through t+5.

title: The outcome is a one-day change in U.S. equity implied volatility, but the paper claims institutional destabilization in markets around the world.
summary: What evidence beyond the one-day VIX change shows that the monetary policy framework, rather than near-term volatility expectations, became less taken for granted after high-BR speeches? The VIX includes risk aversion and does not measure the dispersion of judgments the theory names, the paper does not show whether the rise persists, and it uses no non-U.S. market.
excerpt: Using speeches made by the Chair of the United States Federal Reserve from 1998 to 2014, I proved that reaffirming the assumptions underlying the monetary policy framework causes uncertainty in financial markets around the world.
why: The contribution the paper claims is institutional, but the evidence is a one-day equity volatility association with no measure of the theory's central construct.
settle: Report the backing-ratio coefficient for t+1, t+3, and t+5, add an outcome closer to the framework such as the dispersion of professional rate forecasts, and restate the finding at the scope of the test with a limitations section.

title: The research on Fed speeches is not engaged, and the central theoretical move is already in Harmon, Green and Goodnight (2015).
summary: Is the paper's home central-bank communication, so that it must show what the backing ratio adds to what is known about speeches, or rhetorical institutionalism, so that its contribution is the first test of Harmon et al.'s model? Uncited finance work already finds that coded Fed Chair language forecasts market movements, that Greenspan's speeches have no average market effect, and that central bank speeches matter mainly in the crisis. Prior work also already ties Toulmin's structure to institutional maintenance and change.
excerpt: A key insight of this study is that Toulmin’s linguistic concept of backing can be mapped directly onto institutional theorists’ concept of taken-for-granted assumptions.
sources: contrib-closest (Bligh and Hess 2007; Born, Ehrmann and Fratzscher 2011) stage-2/contribution.md
why: Without the finance literature on Fed speeches a reader cannot tell what the backing ratio adds to known content and tone effects, and the theoretical novelty claim does not hold as written.
settle: State what the backing ratio adds to the Fed-speech findings, present the paper as a test of Harmon et al.'s model and credit it in the theory section, engage the cited and uncited work on explicit legitimation, and drop the "one of the first" wording.

title: The defenses against a slow-moving common cause cannot detect a confounder of the size that would suffice, and the omitted-variable bound is reported at two values.
summary: Drafting one to six months ahead rules out shocks after drafting, not contestation that starts earlier and lasts through the speech. The gap between nearby speeches is about what random pairs would show, and the omitted-variable bound is 0.014 in the text but 0.030 in the figure, with observed covariates already above 0.014.
excerpt: This figure shows that the size of the omitted variable needed to invalidate my results is substantially larger than every other control variable used in existing literature.
why: In a selection-on-observables design these defenses are the whole case against confounding, and as reported they do not reach the kind of confounder the placebo suggests.
settle: Benchmark the pair test against random same-year pairs, regress the backing ratio on lagged slow-moving indicators, and report one omitted-variable bound with its critical value.

title: Because BR is a share of paragraphs, a high-BR speech has little outlook content, and the paper does not test whether that absence explains the result.
summary: The backing ratio is backing paragraphs over all paragraphs, so a high ratio means fewer paragraphs on the economic outlook. Outlook content tends to resolve uncertainty, so this rival predicts the main result from how the measure is built, with the backing contributing nothing.
excerpt: For speeches that discuss the current outlook of the economy (i.e., low BR speeches), writing starts a month before so the most current economic indicators are used.
why: Without a specificity test the mechanism is not identified against a simpler explanation.
settle: Enter the shares of the Toulmin components together with one omitted, or add the outlook-paragraph share beside the backing ratio.

title: Backing-heavy speeches may fall where traders expect the rules to change, and the paper does not control for position in the policy-meeting cycle.
summary: If traders read discussion of the rules as a sign that a rule change is more likely, ordinary asset pricing raises volatility and gives the H1 and H3 signs without any loss of taken-for-grantedness. Fed communication also intensifies before policy meetings, and the paper controls for the last meeting's decision but not for days to the next one.
excerpt: I controlled for expansionary and contractionary monetary policy conditions by creating two dummy variables that were coded “1” if the most recent FOMC meeting resulted in lowering the federal funds rate (i.e., expansionary monetary policy) or raising the federal funds rate (i.e., contractionary monetary policy).
why: A second rival account predicts the main result and one moderator, so H1 cannot yet be credited to the paper's mechanism.
settle: Add days-to-next-meeting fixed effects and a backing-ratio by pre-meeting interaction, and code the backing ratio for a sample of governor speeches to compare slopes.

title: BR is coded with a broad rule by coders whose blinding is not reported, and reliability covers only 70 of the speeches.
summary: Coders who know which speeches moved markets can read policy discussion in those speeches as backing, and that error would correlate with the outcome. Reliability is not reported for the middle 267 speeches or at the speech level the analysis uses.
excerpt: I calculated interrater reliability at the paragraph level (Neuendorf, 2001; Krippendorff, 2003) for the first 60 speeches (Krippendorff’s alpha = 0.88) as well as for the last 10 speeches (Krippendorff’s alpha = .84) to demonstrate consistency.
why: The test assumes the backing ratio measures restatement of taken-for-granted assumptions, and hindsight coding could bias the estimate toward H1.
settle: Publish the codebook, have coders blind to date and speaker re-code a random sample presented out of order, and report the backing-ratio coefficient on the blind codes.

title: The main estimate is at the edge of significance, its stated size is overstated, and the errors ignore speeches that share market days.
summary: The main coefficient supports two stars one-tailed, not three, and is below the effect the design can detect with 80 percent power. One SD of the backing ratio gives about 0.8 percent, not 1.0 percent, and the robust errors make no allowance for speeches on the same or adjacent trading days.
excerpt: Results show robust regressions with robust standard errors in parentheses.
why: A result this close to the threshold is presented as proof, and together with issue 1 the paper cannot show the association is larger on the speech day than before it.
settle: Correct the star and the effect size with intervals, and re-estimate Models 2 to 5 with errors clustered by trading date or week.

title: Every robustness and endogeneity check is described in words, with no coefficients, tables, or appendix.
summary: None of the robustness and endogeneity checks reports a coefficient, standard error, or N, including the two that address the placebo and the policy-news reading. The GEE re-estimation groups speeches by three Chairs in speech order, so it does not address speeches that share trading days.
excerpt: When doing so, I find strong support for all my hypotheses.
why: With a main estimate near the threshold, these checks are the evidence for the robustness claims, and a reader cannot judge any of them.
settle: Add one appendix table with the backing ratio and both interactions under each check, and state the GEE variance type.

title: Some speeches fell on weekends or after the 4 p.m. close, and the paper does not say how they were mapped to trading days.
summary: The Federal Reserve's 2013 speech list includes weekend speeches and at least one framework speech delivered after the close, and the paper does not list its speeches or say how such dates were mapped. For these rows the speech-day change is either a pre-speech change or spans several days.
excerpt: Consistent with work in finance (Chang, Pinegar, and Ravichandran, 1993; Dubois and Louvet, 1996; Choudhry, 2000; Connolly, Stivers, and Sun, 2005), I controlled for day on which the speech took place by creating dummy variables for each weekday.
why: Attributing the VIX change to the speech requires that the outcome window follow the speech, which these rows may not satisfy.
settle: List every Table 2 regressor, report how many speeches fall on weekends, holidays, or after the close and how each was mapped, and re-estimate without them.

title: The sample was trimmed on residuals from an unstated model of the outcome, the count conflicts with the tables, and the estimator is described two ways.
summary: Seven speeches were dropped on outcome residuals, leaving 337 in the text but 339 in every table. Trimming on the outcome selects on the dependent variable, and the text and table note name different estimators.
excerpt: Seven speeches were removed because, based on an outlier analysis, their studentized residuals exceeded plus or minus three.
why: With the main estimate near the threshold, a choice that removes the largest outcome values could decide whether H1 holds.
settle: State the reference model, reconcile 337 and 339, name the estimator, and report Models 2 to 5 on all 344 speeches.

title: The paper does not show how much BR variation is left after 57 other regressors, and topic is coded from the same content as BR.
summary: Model 2 uses 58 regressors on 339 speeches, and topics such as central banking are coded from the same content that defines high-BR speeches. The raw correlation of the backing ratio with the outcome is below the paper's own threshold for significance, so the estimate depends on the controls.
excerpt: To conduct this event study analysis, I used OLS regression with year-fixed effects to estimate the effect of Fed speeches’ BR on market uncertainty.
why: A reader needs to see how much identifying variation remains before accepting the main estimate as a simple finding.
settle: Report the R-squared of the backing ratio on all other regressors, build Model 2 up from the backing ratio alone, and report mean backing ratio by topic.

title: The LIWC positive-tone moderator used for H2 likely measures favorable economic content and speech genre, not emotional tone.
summary: The dictionary's positive words usually describe the economy in Fed speeches, and general dictionaries misclassify financial text. Tone is scored over the whole speech and tracks short ceremonial speeches, so the interaction may not show emotional framing.
excerpt: Positive emotional content is captured using a dictionary approach, whereby the percentage of words psychometrically related to positive emotion (e.g., happy, good, nice, positive, great, favorable, etc.) are reported in relation to all words in a speech.
why: H2 is one of two moderation claims and the practical advice uses it, but the measure may capture content and genre rather than tone.
settle: Report the words that drive the score, re-estimate Models 3 and 5 with tone from non-backing paragraphs and with a finance dictionary, add interactions with word count and topic, and state the LIWC version.

title: The text says that at high positive tone backing "in fact, reduces" uncertainty, but no test of that conditional slope is reported.
summary: The negative slope at high tone is not distinguishable from zero unless the two estimates are strongly negatively correlated, and the covariance is not reported. The figures have no confidence bands, and the 3.5 percent figure at low tone does not follow from the table.
excerpt: Interestingly, when a speech’s positive tone is one standard deviation below its mean, this actually amplifies market uncertainty, increasing the expected range by 3.5 percent.
why: H2 predicts only that tone weakens the effect, so the reversal claim and the advice that uses it go beyond the estimates.
settle: Report the conditional effect of the backing ratio across the observed range of tone and fear with standard errors, state centering and ranges, or narrow the text to attenuation.

title: The business media fear moderator used for H3 is averaged over a window that includes the day after the speech, and it moves with the macro era.
summary: Fear is averaged over the day before through the day after the speech, so two of three days can report on the speech and that day's market move. Fear falls as unemployment rises, the vendor series was back-scored before 2012, and its SD prints as zero. The stated 2.5 percent amplification at one SD of fear is about 1.9 percent by the paper's own figure.
excerpt: I constructed a business media fear variable by taking the average of this fear index over a three-day window (t-1 to t+1) around the day of the speech.
why: A moderator measured partly after the outcome and tied to the macro era cannot show that fear at the time of the speech shapes how traders read it.
settle: Rebuild fear from days before the speech, add interactions with existing uncertainty and the crisis period to Model 5, report H3 before and after 2012, print the SD with enough digits, and correct the H3 effect size.

title: The crisis extension, called "additional validation" in the Discussion, uses estimates that do not fit together and a subsample selected on both moderators.
summary: The crisis-only estimate equals the full-sample estimate, and the crisis interaction p-values hold only on unstated one-tailed tests. The 48-speech reversal comes from a subsample cut on both moderators, including a fear measure taken after the outcome, and the stated model has more parameters than observations. No estimate is reported for the non-crisis years where the theory is said to apply.
excerpt: Interestingly, as additional validation of this story, I also illustrated how, during the financial crisis, when the taken-for-grantedness of these assumptions had weakened, reaffirming them no longer creates uncertainty to the same extent.
why: The Discussion builds a contingent theory and practical advice on this result, which as reported does not show attenuation.
settle: Report Models 2 and 5 for crisis and non-crisis speeches in a table with N and stated tails, list the terms kept for the 48 speeches, show the estimate at other cutoffs, estimate the same high-tone, low-fear cell outside the crisis, or keep the Discussion at the preliminary wording.

title: Thessaly (2008), the source for the mediator step, could not be found.
summary: The only source you cite for the step from lower taken-for-grantedness to more dispersed market judgments, Thessaly (2008), could not be found, and its stated pages overlap another article in that volume.
excerpt: Thus, diminishing the market’s taken-for-grantedness of these assumptions will reduce market participants’ ability to rely on “the way one always does things” to make forecasts about the future, producing greater heterogeneity in overall judgments and decisions made in the market (Thessaly, 2008).
why: The link from the theory to the outcome has no verifiable source.
settle: Replace the citation with a source that can be found or remove it.

title: Brandvold and Halvorsen (2011), the source for central bankers' beliefs, could not be found.
summary: The only scholarly source you cite for central bankers' beliefs, Brandvold and Halvorsen (2011), could not be found, and the Journal of Monetary Economics pages it gives belong to other articles.
excerpt: This empirical setting is particularly noteworthy because the argument I am proposing runs counter to the prevailing wisdom of central bankers (Brandvold and Halvorsen, 2011).
why: The premise the paper argues against has no verifiable scholarly source.
settle: Replace the citation with a source that can be found or remove it.

title: Routine backing conflicts with the premise that backing goes without saying.
summary: The premise that backing "typically goes without saying" conflicts with a sample in which the Chair discusses the backing regularly, and the paper should say how routine backing can still reduce taken-for-grantedness.
excerpt: Given that the backing typically goes without saying, the Chair bringing these assumptions to mind prompts market participants to think about or at least consider the foundations of this framework (Bitektine and Haack, 2015: 58; Harmon, Green, and Goodnight, 2015).
why: The mechanism assumes backing is rare, but the sample shows it is common.
settle: Explain how frequent backing still reduces taken-for-grantedness.

title: The word-count coefficient cannot be read as printed.
summary: The word-count coefficient prints as -0.000 (0.000) in every model, so the Discussion's claim that longer speeches significantly reduce uncertainty cannot be checked; report it per 1,000 words.
excerpt: Specifically, Table 2 indicates that longer speeches significantly reduce market uncertainty.
why: The Discussion's signaling argument uses a coefficient whose size and significance a reader cannot check.
settle: Report the coefficient per 1,000 words with its standard error.

title: The two practical recommendations point in opposite directions.
summary: Which of the two recommendations, wrapping backing in positive language or discussing the assumptions more regularly, does the evidence support, and what result would show that the extra uncertainty deters risk-taking?
excerpt: Perhaps our institutional leaders should discuss these taken-for-granted assumptions more regularly.
why: The practical implications contradict each other and extend past a one-day outcome.
settle: Choose the recommendation the evidence supports and state what would test the long-run claim.

title: Business media fear in Model 4 carries stars its standard error cannot support.
summary: Business media fear in Model 4 is 0.005** with a standard error of 2.924, which cannot be significant and departs from the other models.
excerpt: Significance tests are one-tailed for directional hypotheses, two-tailed for control variables.
why: A printing error in Model 4 raises whether the H3 estimates were printed correctly.
settle: Check and correct the Model 4 entry.

title: The Model 5 adjusted R-squared does not follow from its R-squared.
summary: The Model 5 adjusted R-squared of 0.261 does not follow from its R-squared of 0.355 with 339 observations and 60 df, which give 0.216.
excerpt: All models include year, topic, and local audience fixed-effects.
why: A table value does not reproduce.
settle: Correct the adjusted R-squared.

title: Text-only estimates label their uncertainty as a variance.
summary: The uncertainty of every text-only estimate is labeled "σ2," which reads as a variance, so the reader cannot tell whether it is a standard error.
excerpt: The interaction term reaches marginal significance (β = -0.051, σ2 = 0.038, p = .088, adjusted R-squared = 0.191).
why: The supplemental tests cannot be recomputed from the label as written.
settle: Label the values as standard errors if they are.

title: Stars on the positive-tone main effect fit one-tailed tests only.
summary: The stars on the positive-tone main effect require one-tailed tests, but the Table 2 note says controls are tested two-tailed.
excerpt: Significance tests are one-tailed for directional hypotheses, two-tailed for control variables.
why: The table's stars do not follow its own stated tests.
settle: Apply the stated two-tailed test to the stars.

title: Audience fixed effects do not address attention within audience categories.
summary: Audience fixed effects remove only five category means, so within-category differences in attention (a flagship venue versus a routine event) remain; a t0 newswire count per speech and its interaction with BR would address this.
excerpt: All models include year, topic, and local audience fixed-effects.
why: High-BR speeches may go to venues that draw more market attention.
settle: Add a speech-level newswire count on the speech day and its interaction with the backing ratio.

title: The paper does not say which traders hold the framework as taken for granted.
summary: Under your mechanism, should traders who follow Fed policy closely react more or less to backing than other market participants, and can you show which group moves the VIX on high-BR days?
excerpt: This relationship is likely due to the fact that higher levels of sophistication are potentially required to understand the complexities and implications of the assumptions underlying the Fed’s monetary policy framework.
why: The mechanism does not say whose taken-for-grantedness changes.
settle: State the prediction for informed traders and test it if the data allow.

title: The model has no Chair fixed effects.
summary: The model has no Chair fixed effects or BR x Chair term, although three Chairs with very different speech counts may differ in BR and in how markets read them.
excerpt: The final sample thus consisted of 337 speeches (159 by Alan Greenspan, 166 by Ben Bernanke, and 12 by Janet Yellen) (see Figure 2).
why: Speaker differences may enter the backing-ratio estimate.
settle: Add Chair fixed effects and a backing-ratio by Chair interaction.

title: The VIX measures the size of expected moves, not their direction.
summary: The paper describes the VIX as traders' estimate of the direction of the S&P 500, but it measures the expected size of moves, so the emotion argument about optimistic and pessimistic directions is not tested by it.
excerpt: The VIX thus represents options traders’ estimates of the direction of the S&P 500 over the next month by providing an aggregate measure of the variance of option prices on any given day.
why: The outcome does not measure what the emotion argument predicts.
settle: Correct the description and test direction with returns if the argument is kept.

title: Signaling theory appears only in the Discussion.
summary: Signaling theory, which holds the view the paper argues against, appears only in the Discussion, while the introduction's foil is a practitioner belief.
excerpt: My primary finding also appears to be somewhat at odds with signaling theory (Akerlof, 1970; Spence, 1973), which is arguably the most dominant theory for understanding how communication influences financial markets (Tetlock, 2007; Graffin, Carpenter, and Boivie, 2011).
why: The introduction does not name the theory the paper challenges.
settle: Introduce signaling theory as the foil in the introduction.

title: The gap statement does not say what existing theory gets wrong.
summary: The introduction justifies the study by saying we still know little about leaders who reaffirm assumptions, without saying what existing theory gets wrong about this case.
excerpt: As a result, we still know little about the institutional consequences of leaders who try to reinforce the existing social order by simply reaffirming these assumptions directly.
why: An unstudied topic is a weaker motivation than a stated problem with prior theory.
settle: State what prior theory predicts for this case and why it may be wrong.

title: The promised reversal is recast as complementary in the Discussion.
summary: The introduction promises an unconditional reversal of the prevailing intuition, but the Discussion recasts the finding as complementary to it under a condition that is never measured.
excerpt: In this sense, my findings are not in opposition to this original intuition, but rather, complementary to it in that together they portray a more holistic story about the relationship between language and institutionalization.
why: The introduction and Discussion make different claims.
settle: Align the introduction's claim with the Discussion.

title: The Fedspeak controls come from dictionaries validated elsewhere.
summary: The four language controls used to rule out Fedspeak come from dictionaries validated in other domains, and the partial vagueness dictionary is not specified.
excerpt: I controlled for speech complexity by using the Flesch-Kincaid reading grade level (Kincaid et al., 1975); speech abstractness by using a word dictionary compiled and validated by Mergenthaler (1996); and speech vagueness by using a partial dictionary compiled and validated by Hiller and colleagues (1969).
why: The controls may not capture the obfuscation they are meant to rule out.
settle: Specify the vagueness dictionary and discuss the controls' validity for Fed speech.

title: The interactions assume a linear change in the backing-ratio slope.
summary: Both interactions use a single linear product term, with no binned or flexible check that the BR slope changes linearly with tone or fear.
excerpt: Model 3 adds the first interaction term between the BR and speech positive tone.
why: The moderation estimates assume a functional form the paper does not check.
settle: Report a binned estimator of the backing-ratio slope across tone and fear.

title: The moderator hypotheses add an incremental contribution.
summary: H2 and H3 extend Pfarrer, Pollock and Rindova (2010), as the paper says, so the space they take might go to the H1 mechanism, with the moderators as secondary analyses.
excerpt: However, I suggest that while the overall positive tone of a speech may indeed influence market evaluations directly, more importantly, it may also function as an interpretive context that shapes how market participants collectively make sense of specific ideas that the Fed Chair is discussing (Pfarrer, Pollock, and Rindova, 2010).
why: Space spent on the moderators is not spent on the main mechanism.
settle: Move H2 and H3 to secondary analyses.

title: Ease-of-retrieval research offers a testable micro-mechanism.
summary: Research on ease of retrieval in persuasion offers a tested micro-mechanism for H1 and a moderator, audience elaboration, that the paper could use or rule out.
excerpt: Recall that Hypothesis 1 contends that when the Fed Chair begins to reaffirm the backing explicitly, this will prompt market participants to think of alternatives to the current way of doing things and lead them to make decisions in increasingly diverging directions.
why: The micro-foundation of H1 is stated but not connected to tested work.
settle: Discuss the ease-of-retrieval account and the moderator it implies.

title: The VXX translation does not follow from the coefficient.
summary: The VXX translation does not follow from a spot-VIX coefficient, because the VXX began trading in 2009 and its issuer states it will not necessarily track the VIX.
excerpt: A $10,000 investment would hypothetically gross a one-day return of $100 (1 percent).
why: The practical-significance example overstates what the estimate implies.
settle: Remove the VXX example or restate it in VIX units.

title: The location dummy has an impossible SD.
summary: Table 1 prints an SD of 0.64 for the Washington, D.C. location dummy, which is impossible for a 0/1 variable with mean 0.29.
excerpt: I created a dummy variable for the speech location by assigning a “1” to speeches given in Washington, D.C., which is the Fed’s headquarters and the meeting location of the FOMC.
why: A table value is impossible as printed.
settle: Correct the SD in Table 1.

title: Loughran and McDonald (2011) is misspelled.
summary: The reference list misspells McDonald as "McDonaold" in Loughran and McDonald (2011).
excerpt: Loughran, T., and B. McDonaold 2011 “When Is a Liability Not a Liability? Textual Analysis, Dictionaries, and 10-Ks.” The Journal of Finance, 66: 35–65.
why: A citation error.
settle: Correct the spelling in the text and reference list.

title: The Kincaid et al. (1975) author record did not match.
summary: Please confirm the author list for Kincaid et al. (1975); the database record did not match, possibly because the record itself is garbled.
excerpt: Kincaid, J. P., R. P. Fishburne Jr, R. L. Rogers, and B. S. Chissom 1975 Derivation of new readability formulas (automated readability index, fog count and flesch reading ease formula) for navy enlisted personnel.
why: A possible citation error.
settle: Confirm the authors against the Navy report.
